image_description:
**1. Chart type**  
- **Stacked area chart** (time series), with many sub-areas for origins/countries and broader color-coded regional groupings.

**2. Layout techniques**  
- **Stacking** is used to show how components add up to the total share over time.  
- No faceting or small multiples.  
- Includes **vertical reference lines/annotations** for 1921 and 1965.

**3. Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Share of the U.S. population that was born abroad | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; total stacked height |
| Place of birth / origin group (individual countries or origins shown as stacked bands, e.g., Ireland, Germany, Canada, Mexico) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked area bands; labels inside bands |
| World region (e.g., Asia, Europe, Americas, Africa, Middle East, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of stacked areas; right-side labels |
| Immigration policy event year (1921, 1965) | Temporal | Vertical dashed reference lines |
| Immigration policy event description | Categorical/nominal (text annotation) | Text labels attached to reference lines |

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the relationship between the passage of time and the percentage of Americans born abroad, with relation to two variables. The graph shows that we had a high percentage (10-15%) of foreign-born Americans between 1850 and 1910 (most of these immigrants were Canadian, Irish, and German). Then in 1921 Congress introduced quotas per country on immigration. This put a limit on the amount of people from each country that could be granted citizenship per year. This saw a plummet in all immigration until it was rolled back in 1965. After 1965, through to 2010, the percentage went back up to 10-15. The immigrants, however, were from different countries. The main countries on the part were Mexico and extraneous areas of Asia and Europe (as well as small amounts of Middle Easterners and Africans).

comments.raw_comment:
Immigration: The Heart of America

In this graph, I notice that from 1921 to 1965 the percent of U.S. population that was born abroad rapidly decreased. According to the graph, this is because Congress created country-based immigration quotas. I also noticed that beginning in the 1970s, the U.S. population started to consist of people from Africa, the Middle East, and Mexico. 

From looking at this graph, I wonder why most of the immigrants from 1850 to 1921 were from Ireland and Germany. What was the reason for their immigration? This graph also makes me wonder why immigrants from Asia and ‘other’ areas came mostly in the 1970s and so on. Was there a specific reason for their lack of immigration to the U.S. before the 1970s? 

This graph represents the percentage of the U.S. population that was born abroad. It follows immigration to the U.S. starting in the 1850s and continuing until 2010. Each prominent country is represented by a color and it either declines or increases, depending on what was going on in their country at the time, or what rules/regulations the U.S. had passed regarding immigration. 

This graph relates to me because my father is a child of an immigrant. His mother lived in Italy, but decided to immigrate to America after World War II. This graph also relates to my community because most of the people around me have stemmed from immigrants. We all have some sort of story to share on how our family’s reached America and it bonds us as a community.

1. This graph shows the population of the United States that was born abroad from the year 1850 to 2010. Ireland and Germany were very much where most people born abroad lived in America in 1850. Then, when country-based immigration quotas were created, all percentages went down, meaning that many fewer immigrants or non-American-born people were coming in. Then, when these quotas were rolled back, Mexico became the leading country where immigrants in America were born from. 
2.  I wonder why the percentage of the US population that was born abroad in America did not go down immediately after the country-based immigration quotas were created. Similarly, I wonder why the percentages did not instantly increase after these quotas were pushed back. 
3. This relates to me and my community because while I was born in America, it is interesting and important to learn about the other countries in which people in America were born. It is also important to learn what created increases and decreases in the percentages of the US population that were born abroad. 
New title: From Where and When People Came to America

Is America truly a "Melting Pot"?

Within this graph, the first thing that I noted was that the percentage of immigrants/foreign people living within the US, steadily declined after the quotas were initiated by congress. Until they rolled back on these quotas is when immigration started to increase yet again. Especially within This influx (and efflux), leads me to question what steps congress took to implement quotas and why did they feel the need to implement them. I also wonder how people of other religions/races/ethnicities, or people who were solely immigrating to begin with reacted to these drawbacks. This affects my community because America is considered to be a “melting pot” and because of the outflow of many races and ethnicities, the country lacks that representation and that reputation of being inclusive.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, the percentage of how many US residents were born in different countries is represented per year. From 1850-1921. the graph is pretty steady with a majority of immigrants coming from Europe. Then, in 1921 Congress created country-based immigration quotas and the total number of immigrants drops from around 15% to roughly 5%. From 1965 (when Congress rolled back the quotas)- 2015 the graph increases to 15% of the US population being immigrants. However, the distribution has changed dramatically. Firstly, the vast majority of immigrants coming into the US are now from Mexico. Europe's percentage has also significantly decreased, only taking up about 1/8 of all immigrants to the US. Asia has also increased to roughly that size.

This graph also makes me wonder where in the US did these different immigrants settle? Did they evenly spread out, or did people of the same nationality settle in neighboring places? This graph relates to me and my community personally because my grandparents immigrated from Ireland in the late 50s/ early 60s, so right before Congress rolled back on quotas. This graph represents the percentage of the United States population that was born abroad. The three most prevalent categories are red which represents the Americas, yellow which represents Europe, and blue which represents Asia. The x-axis shows how the populations from these countries increase as time passes. I also notice that in 1921 the graph says that Congress announced the creates of country-based immigration quotas. After this the population of the Americas and Europe steadily decreased until 1965 when the quotas were rolled back.

I wonder why even after the immigration quotas were rolled back the immigration from Europe continued to decrease.

I observed that while the immigration from Europe and the Americas decreased after the immigration quotas of 1921, the immigrants from other countries began to rise. After the roll back the immigration from the Americans greatly increased, however instead of the majority of immigrants being from Canada, a majority were now from Mexico. In addition, to this after the quota roll backs immigration from Asia greatly increased. 

Like so many others in the country my grandparents had immigrated to America. Therefore, this graph relates to me in the sense that it represents the ways that diversity in immigration is so deeply entwined in America.

This graph shows the percentage of foreign people from each continent living in the USA from the year 1850 to 2010.

What do you notice?
I notice that the percentage had a noticeable drop between 1920 and 1960. Posible due to the quotas set by the congress on 1921,  because when they called them off the percentage started to rise again. The percentage of Europeans was the higher one during the late XIX century and almost all of XX century.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if Germany's role in both World Wars had something to do with the decrease on the country's percentage that started near to the dates of World War I, and an even greater drop starting around World War II.
Also that if before 1965 there weren't quotas for Africa and Middle East immigrants and that's why there wasn't a percentage.
I wonder what were the factors of the increase in Mexico's  percentage during the last decades, and if it has to do with the 1994 economic crisis, because even though the rise started decades before that, it might have something to do with it.

How does this relate to you and your community?
It relates because the main percentage on 2010 is Mexico's and as a Mexican myself I ponder why is 
But maybe it could be about other non-economical factors.

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
"Foreign percentage in the US"

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
After Congress instated the quotas, the U.S. population born abroad significantly decreased. It continued to decrease pretty sharply. When Congress rolls back the quotas, there is a sharp increase in the graph. 

What do you wonder?
Why did Congress put the quotas in place? What made them decide to take away these quotas? Did other countries take similar courses of action during these times? 

How does this relate to you and your community?
I come from a family of immigrants, and I live in a community that is primarily first or second-generation in the US. Ellis Island opened around the time that Congress rolled back on the quotas. My grandpa and some of my friend's grandparents went through Ellis Island. The roll back likely allowed them to come to the US.

What do I notice? 
I noticed that in the late 1800s and early 1900s, most of the U.S. population born abroad was from Europe, specifically a large majority from Ireland and Germany. There was a significant spike in Irish immigrants in the 1850s when the Irish Potato Famine occurred. In 1921, the government created a country-based immigration quota, and there was a sharp decrease in the U.S. population born abroad. After Congress rolled back the quota, there was a sharp increase in immigrants from Mexico and Asia. 
What do I wonder?
I wonder why there is a slight increase in African and middle eastern people born abroad who now live in the U.S. in the 2000s. I also wonder what was happening in the countries that many people emigrated from that would cause them to come to America. Lastly, I wonder what the next ten years will look like on this graph. 
How this relates to my community
My community is constantly changing, specifically a change in people of different races. My town has a sizeable Paraguayan population that has become an integral part of my community.

comments.raw_comment:
1.) What do I notice? 
I notice that each color is intended to represent a continent or region of origin, separated into countries by lightly colored lines. The thickness of a color represents the share of the U.S. population (percentage) that originated from that region. 

2.) What do I wonder? 
I wonder how having additional historical context (such as when wars or major historical events started) marked on the graph would give context to the reasons for increases in immigration. It would also explain the changes in why certain countries had the most immigrants at any given time. Also, (and maybe this is connected), I wonder why the lowest immigration numbers coincide with the U.S.’s rollback of immigration quotas–intuitively, this should be the opposite of the expected result.
 
3.) How does this affect me and my community? 
Immigration in the United States affects all people because these immigrants are the people joining our communities, and we interact with them on a daily basis.
 
4.). Can you create a catchy headline for this graph?
The Rise and Fall of Immigrant Origins

 In the beginning ,  Places like Germany and Italy were rife with violence, and Ireland was facing a famine, so these people had no other choice but to flee their country.

 It's important to know the demographics of the community regardless if you are trying to survey them, or just want to be an active member of your community.  It's important to understand how much of the US population is not native to America, as well as how these values changed over time.

I immediately noticed the decline of immigrants from the creation of the immigration quotas to the end of the quotas. Prior to 1965, most immigrants in the United States were from Ireland, Germany, as well as Canada. Then from 1965 and forward, there was a shift in demographics. There is a constant increase of immigrants from Asia and the Americas, especially Mexico. 

What factors caused this shift? And what caused the population of Irish immigrants to decline and not “bounce back” after the quota system rolled back? Perhaps the growing U.S. economy, education, safety and refuge from the Vietnam War, and new opportunities contributed to the surge of immigrants. 

These population changes affect my community in many ways. It increases population, diversity, economic output and growth. It also makes me wonder what the future holds for immigration rates. 

Headline: U.S. Immigration in Waves

comments.raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the change in immigration from the year 1850 to after 2010.  In the 1800s, there was a large amount of Irish and German immigrants and a small amount of Canadians.  In 1920, the US government implemented an immigration act that set quotas for how many immigrants could come from each country.  In the 60s, this quota was taken away and immigration began to rise again.  On the right side of the second line, the largest group is no longer Europe, but rather Mexico and Canada.  The main thing that stands out is the large decrease after the quota was put in place.  It was probably very difficult for people to come to America at this time.  I wonder what caused the shift in what people were immigrating.  I wonder if wars in Asia had anything to do with this increase in their immigration after the quota was dropped.  Immigration is relevant to the community because people from new places are constantly coming to America and it is important to be aware of the situation.  I would call this, "A Shift in Immigration Demographics"

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph displays the distribution of the foreign-born residents by country of origin for the period 1850 – 2019.  You can see the interactive version with statistics for 50+ countries toward the bottom of article linked athttps://tinyurl.com/USIbyC.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph.  We look forward to replying to your discoveries.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included this graph.  

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Oct. 21 with moderation on Wednesday, Oct. 26.  The topic – income mobility of children of immigrants.

I noticed that the United State’s population in the 19th century had predominantly Irish and German immigrants. By 1950, European immigrants were still dominating as the highest but they are not as far off as the other continents. I noticed by the 21st century, Mexican immigrants have the highest foreign-born share. I notice that none of the continents have remained consistent as they either show a dramatic increase or decrease or recently appeared on the graph. 

I wonder why Africa and the Middle East only began to show in the foreign-born share in the 1970s. Did it have to do with immigration laws prior to the 1965’s congress decision to roll back quotas? I also wonder why Germany and Ireland share almost the same amount of the foreign base share. It makes me wonder if they traveled together and if these countries had an alliance/purpose to come to America.  

 It affects my community because it spreads awareness about the history of quotas, how this applies today, and federal legislation that can be in place to provide better opportunities/accessibility for immigrants. 

 Catchy Headline: The Continental Journey

comments.raw_comment: One thing I noticed was the significant decrease in immigrants in the population after congress created country-based immigration quotas. This makes me wonder how the government came up with these cap numbers. I imagine they would use country population sizes and percent of immigrants already in the US population to decide how many more immigrants they can accept from each country every year. However, I wonder if racism also factored into this decision. For example, we learned about the Chinese Exclusion Act which prohibited all immigration of Chinese workers for ten years. Perhaps this accounted for why the population of Asian immigrants is lower than immigrants from other continents. I also noticed that data about African immigrants doesn’t go all the way back to the 1850s and seems to start as late as the 1970s. This makes me wonder if data on African immigrant populations doesn’t exist before then. We learned about how African Americans' lineages can be very difficult to trace. This is largely a result of slavery since many slaves didn’t have birth and death certificates. This graph relates to me because both my parents are immigrants. My mom is from the Philippines and my dad is from England, and it’s interesting to see where they fit into the graph when they immigrated in the 1990s. They both came here for work and better opportunities which is the driving force for immigrants from many different countries. My catchy headline for this graph is “Immigration Nation”.

This has the impact of informing me and my community of where people immigrate from. It also has the impact of informing me and my community that immigration quotas are effective.

comments.raw_comment: 1. I notice that from around 1860 to 1920, there were more immigrants from Canada. I wonder what may have changed to cause them to not immigrate as much later, for example, from the 1960s to 2020-ish. There aren't nearly as many immigrants after Congress rolls back quotas. However, we do see a huge rise in immigrants from Mexico, but not that many earlier on. This inverse correlation is interesting, and I wonder why there aren't as many Canadian immigrants later. Also, earlier, there were lots of Irish, German, and other Europeans recorded as immigrants. To top it off, there are many more Middle Eastern, African, and Asian immigrants near the end. I can see the line for Asia, and I think I can hardly see, but still kind of see, the line for Africa and the Middle East. This relates to my community because my community is made up of people. If more people in my community are immigrants, they bring with them things from their culture, religion, they bring customs, and they influence other people with their ideas. This is actually very important. If we never see or get to know people from other countries, cultures, and religions, we might make incorrect judgement on them and misunderstand some things they may do or believe. Immigrants can help people get a clearer view of what's happening in other countries. There is a possibility this may improve relationships between other countries and people who are different than you are.

comments.raw_comment:
As everyone will probably have noticed, many people came to America after congress rolled back the quotas on immigrants. I have also noticed, and perhaps others have as well, that immigration from certain countries increases whenever that country isn't stable. Then everyone rushes to a stable country, which in this case is America. 

     Now, I wonder what purpose congress might have had in mind to put in strict quotas, and then loosen them. Their purpose has to have failed, for why else would you loosen them. 

     This matters to me for my family, my friends, and I are all immigrants, and if congress tightens the quotas again, we might get sent back and away from home.  

     A good title for this graph could be "Immigration throughout the 1850s-2010s".

comments.raw_comment: When looking at the model, I realize a few intersting things. Prior to the enactment of the 1921 country-based Immigration Quota, there was a larger proportion of Irish and Germans immigrants. This is sensible considering that during the latter half of the 19th century, the Irish potato famine resulted in a mass exodus of people seeking a better life in the US. Same with Germany, as economic hardship, religious persecution, and violent revolutions have caused millions to flee during a similar time period. Immigration remained consistent after the enactment of the quotas until the quotas were lifted in 1965.What is interesting after 1965 was that the primary country of immigration was no longer dominated by the Europeans, but rather by China, Canada, and Mexico. This is indicative of the shift in economic hardship that took place in the world of the past century. While Europe was stabilizing, Mexico and China began to falter. A major increase of North American immigration started to pick up during the 1990s during the commencement of Industrial Westernization, otherwise know as the process of moving factories form North America, to China. Mexico's economy collapse after this, and many sought better economic opportunity in the states.

comments.raw_comment: I notice the period between 1850-1870 was when the largest amount of people in the US population was born abroad, at around 15%. I wonder why the percentage was at its peak then? It could be attributed to the fact that the US was still a relatively new country, and many perceived the U.S. to have lots of opportunities. I notice that in the earliest 50-ish that the graph depicts, a large chunk of the US population that was born abroad came from Ireland. I wonder if it was because of the potato famine at that time. I also notice that following a spike in immigration during the 1910s, Congress established immigration quotas that directly led to a significant decrease in the share of the US population that was born abroad. I noticed that after Congress rolled back the immigration quotas, there was a drop in the US population that was born in Europe, and an increase in immigration from the Americas and Asia. I wonder what led Congress to enact and eventually revoke their immigration quotas; what kind of measures were they looking at that influenced their decision? I see that starting around the 2000s, there were more immigrants from the Middle East and Africa when prior to that time period they weren’t even visible on the graph. I wonder what caused more immigration from these areas. I wonder what this graph will look like in the coming years--what regions or countries will become more prominent on the graph, and will there be a new peak percentage of the population born abroad?

comments.raw_comment:
The main purpose of this graph it to suggest that creating immigration quotas works in controlling the flow of immigrants. Though, this plot hides the percentage of illegal immigrants.

A few comments about what happens after 1968.

I don't think that we can reach conclusions about the mechanisms of the changes without looking at the absolute numbers that make the percentages. A change in the percentage can be due to increase/decrease of the immigration rate and/or to a decrease/increase of the native population (e.g. due to changes in the birth rate). 

If we had to assume that the US native population is constant over time (i.e. population growth is due only to immigrants, at least in the post WW2 time), and in the context of growing world population (doubled in the last 50 years) we see that Europe (no population growth) has an apparent decrease in the share of immigrants compared to other regions (e.g. Asia and Africa) whose population is growing rapidly. This may indicate that the change in immigration pressure is simply due to changes in demographic pressure. 

We may also attribute the growth in the share of immigrants from the Americas as due to the bad economic conditions in most of the latin-american countries after 1990.

- I notice that before 1921 most of the immigrants were from Canada, Ireland, and Germany. What do you wonder?

How does this relate to you and your community?

Also, a large percentage of my community is Mexican, which were a large percentage of the increase after 1965. Another reason why this relates to me is because the percentage of immigrants/ Mexicans include my parents who came to the US to live and give us a better life. 

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
- The graph shows the percentage of immigrants over the years, where they're from, and what happened before/after congress created/rolled back immigration quotas.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed that initially it was mainly Europeans who were immigrating to the U.S. in the late 1800's and early 1900's. Another observation I made was that starting in the mid to late 1900's, immigration started to increase, but now from other areas of the world, such as from Asia, and Africa, as well as a sharp increase of people from Mexico. Lastly, immigration quotas resulted in a drastic drop in immigration to the U.S., until those quotas were rolled back.
2. I wonder what caused the huge influx of Irish, German, and Canadian immigrants to the United States. What political or economic circumstances caused all these people to leave their homes, did all these people positively or negatively impact the United States, these are things I wonder about. I can relate this to statistics in the sense that the more instability a country is experiencing, the more likely it is that people are to leave. 
3. This relates to my community because the increase of Mexicans to the United States probably resulted in me being an American citizen. My parents immigrated from Mexico to here, and that is why I have the privilege of being an American citizen. They probably took note of everyone else leaving their homes and making their way to the U.S. and decided to go as well. I also have to take into account the state of Mexico and the events taking place as well. 
4. Surf's up! Experience the immigration wave of history as you hang ten with others who took on the same treacherous feat!

I also noticed that a large percentage of the U.S population that was born abroad are from Europe while the lowest percentage seems to belong to the middle east, but it’s very close to Africa's percentage. I noticed that after creating immigration quotas in 1925 all of the lines took a dip and then after retracting the quotas in 1965 they picked back up again. It can be said that the quotas and the population of people born abroad have a negative correlation.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why certain continents don’t have any countries listed like the Americas and Europe. For instance, there are no countries included for Asia or Africa. I wonder if it’s because there’s such a small amount that specific countries can’t be identified or if it's due to another reason. I also wonder why immigration quotas were made in the first place and why they were taken back by Congress.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because it gives insight into the U.S population which includes all of us in America. And there are several people who were born abroad and came to the country to eventually live in Perth amboy which would include some of my friends and a lot of my family.

What do you notice?
I noticed that once Congress created country-based immigration quotas in 1921,  the percentage of immigration overall would decrease. Before that, Ireland would have most of the population in the U.S. in the graph. But then in 1965 when Congress rolled back the quotas, immigration started going up again. Mexico started immigrating more to the U.S. after that. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what were the reasons for people to immigrate to the U.S. and if they had similar situations. For example, could it have been that they wanted freedom? Not only that but if the immigration quotas weren't created, would the share of U.S. population percentage have gone past 15% for a country. I also wonder if this graph includes both legal and illegal immigration from the countries. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because here in Perth Amboy there are a lot of immigrants, including my parents. There are mainly hispanics in the community. In the graph, there have been more Mexicans immigrating to the U.S.. This trend could explain why over the years, there have been more hispanics, especially mexicans, residing in Perth Amboy or in neighboring cities. 

What’s going on in this graph? 
In this graph, it shows the share of the U.S. population that immigrants from different places have. A catch line would be: “Get your share in the U.S. population”

1. I notice that during the years 1850 to 1910 most of the population from abroad was either from Canada, Ireland, or Germany. Their presence was huge with 10 to 15%. Then after Congress creates the quotas, the immigrant population decreases dramatically until it's at or less than 5%. comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that in the years 1850 through 1910, almost 15% of the U.S. population was from Canada and Europe which were from Ireland and Germany in specific. After congress established the immigration quotas, the percent of the population born abroad was on a consistent decrease from 1921 to 1965. Since the quotas were rolled back, the population born abroad had changed to Mexico, Africa, Middle East and Asia.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if the U.S. rolled back the quotas due to an economic impact from the decrease of immigrants? I also wonder if a change in living situation in Asia caused them to move to the United States.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because living in a very diverse area, this was only possible because the quotas have been rolled back. My family is a contribution to the increase of population born abroad and since my community is mostly made of hispanics who are immigrants as well, areas like these are the ones who hold most of the U.S. populations born abroad. 
What's going on in the graph? Create a catchy headline.
In the graph, in the earlier years, Canada and Europe made up almost 15% of the U.S. population born abroad and as congress created immigration quotas the percentages plummeted. Since a roll back in the quotas, new continents have made an increase in the population born abroad. 
The U.S. Sees A Rise After A Steep Decrease In Population Born Abroad

comments.raw_comment:
1. Prior to 1921, I observe that Europeans, particularly those from Germany and Ireland, had a high immigration population rate. Only 2% of immigrants were Canadian, making up both nations for around 13% of all immigrants. These three populations started to decline after 1921, and in 1965 a significant shift was shown. With up to 8% of the 15% of immigrants living in the United States, Mexico has emerged as the major source of immigration.
2. I'm curious as to what factors led to the shift from Europeans to Mexicans as the most prevalent immigrant group. Does the decline in immigrant populations between 1921 and 1965 have anything to do with deportations? What would the immigrant demographic be like if the quotas were never approved by Congress?
3. Since I am a child of immigrants who left El Salvador to avoid conflict, corruption, and financial problems, this affects me and my community. Since it was so dangerous in El Salvador in the 1980s, my parents came to the United States to work and try to give their children an opportunity to have a better life than they did. This demonstrates that many immigrants come to this country for a variety of reasons simply in order to improve their standard of living for themselves and their family. The percentage of Mexicans in the population is especially significant because they are a crucial component of both the Hispanic community and this country.
4. “An Integral Part of U.S Diversity: Immigration Numbers on the Rise”

What do you notice? I noticed that with the implementation of policies such as country-based immigration quotas in 1921, the amount of immigration decreased until 1965. However, in 1965, with the removal of such a policy, immigration increased again. Also, in the beginning, most of the share of U.S immigrants were from Europe and Canada. However, after 1965, it belongs mostly to Mexico and Asia. I believe the percentage of immigration is different, because of some factors related to the country of origin such as the quality of life, war (world war 1), and internal problems. Also, it depends on some factors about the U.S, such as the hospitality, and acceptability of the country of destination, and the U.S towards such immigrants.

What do you wonder?  I wonder what was the motivation of such immigration from the countries of origin, was it mostly to financial problems or related to the factors such as freedom of speech? But my main question is that if it was not a policy between 1921, and 1965 was it possible that we have seen another peak, such as the peak that we can see in 1914? If the policy was the main reason for the reduction in immigration? Is this graph includes illegal immigration?

How does this relate to you and your community?  It explains the current diversity of U.S. The percentage of immigration from Canada decreased.

What’s going on in this graph?  Is the United States really diverse?
